newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish budget too optimistic on growth-economists.
newsitem.headline: Finnish budget too optimistic on growth-economists.

text.p: The Finnish 1997 state budget is a shade too optimistic on growth and the deficit, but the government deserves praise for its relentless drive towards fiscal consolidation, economists said on Tuesday.

The five-party government brought its 191 billion markka budget proposal to parliament, saying strong economic growth would put Finland in a good position to meet the entry criteria for Economic and Monetary Union in 1997.
"The air is rife with friendly winds," Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto told Reuters.
But four bank economists said the budget was based on an overly optimistic 3.9-percent gross domestic growth forecast.
"The growth forecast is slightly too optimistic," said Interbank economist Sampsa Laine.
In addition, "their expectation for the investment trend is very optimistic," said Ari Aaltonen, chief economist at Postipankki, referring to the government's 10.5 percent 1997 forecast.
Economists said if growth failed to materialise at the pace projected by the government, the estimated 1997 budget deficit of 28.8 billion markka would increase.

"The net borrowing requirement set by the finance ministry could prove quite optimistic," said Jorma Vanninen, economist at OKOBANK. The deficit could well become "a few billion markka" bigger, he said.

But Esko Torsti, head of market advisory at Enskilda in Helsinki, said the crucial thing was that even with a slightly bigger than forecast budget deficit, Finland would meet the deficit criterion for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Financial markets expect Finland to decide to link the markka to Europe's ERM this autumn. A peg could lead to a further fall in long-term bond yields, economists said.

Economists said no immediate impact on interest rates or the markka exchange rate was expected from the budget or the EMU convergence programme released with it since key parts of the documents had already been published a couple of weeks ago.

The 10-year bond yield gap over Bunds has narrowed 25 basis points to 72 bps from 97 bps on August 15, the day before the government agreed on the budget. Economists said the narrowing of the differential gap could partly be attributed to credibility in the coalition's policies.
But they noted that the government's interest rate forecast in 1997 might be on the optimistic side.
The government sees short-term Helibor market interest rates steady at 3.8 percent, five-year bond yields unchanged at 6.3 percent and 10-year bond yields unchanged at 7.3 percent.
"I think they are a bit too optimistic regarding long-term interest rates," Interbank's Laine said.
But Torsti said "looking purely at domestic components the (projected) interest rate level is realistic."
Economists particularly praised income tax breaks worth 5.5 billion markka in 1997.
"The government has done a good job...the structural decisions, primarily on income taxation, are in the right direction," Torsti said.
"That extra cut in income taxes was positive, a strong signal, which will cheer the home-market," Vanninen said.
